Digital Innovation 3 – תמלול נקי

Product innovation. And product innovation is hard. At the end of the day, we wanna have a business. We wanna sell, we wanna create a company, we wanna succeed. So what are the challenges of taking an idea, a concept, an innovation, and moving it into the market? So that will be what we are gonna focus this week. There's a lot of material. I might not finish today. We'll continue next week.

But let's start with, first of all, covering what we did last week. So just for two minutes, what we did last week is we understood that innovation is usually an incremental process. So once there are the enablers, what I called them last week, then a lot of people, many, many times more than one person, takes the next step and invents something. Whether it is Darwin or whether it was Edison, whether it was all the other people, they usually, when the enablers were in place, many people invented and moved to the next step.

Second thing that we saw was that these innovations usually were identical. So people came in with the same exact ideas on how to move forward. So the question is, of course, when these innovations come, what happens? So one of the things that is fairly amazing is that companies that are entrenched in the market, big companies, when there is an innovation called a disruptive innovation, and we'll talk about it later, they somehow fail to recognize the problem. They don't respond to it, and they lose the market.

And the question was, why? Why companies with very, very good managers, smart people that build companies that are very large and very successful lose out? You know, it doesn't make any sense because these people know what they're doing. They built a company to begin with. They were the kings of the hill for ten years, fifty years, and they lose. Why do they lose? And the product innovation succeeds when the product reaches acceptable levels of price, performance, and ease of use, and that will be a key issue that we'll discuss today.

We talked about innovations, smartphone. There are many more useful apps that we can develop on phones, and especially if we move to business applications. What can we do in order to build an innovation? Here's an area where people who are interested in coming up with the next innovation. You have the enabler. The phone is a very, very big enabler. It's connected to the internet twenty-four/seven, and you can use it in a lot of business applications. A lot of the stories I heard about why smartphones spread so rapidly around the world, including in Central Africa. Well, they don't have computers in Central Africa. They have farmers.

So it turns out that farmers in Central Africa use the smartphone in order to find the price of cocoa or coffee or coffee beans using their smartphone. So because everything is connected, people use it for a lot of business applications, even if we don't think about it.

We have all these platforms. I talked a little bit about ChatGPT. ChatGPT is a great example of innovation that we don't really know what's gonna happen with it. And we talked about all of that. I missed the product innovation, which is how to use this technology and where and when to use it. And I've got examples in here how this technology impacts many, many industries. So you look at movie theater, you look at postage service, you have a lot of these places.

We're gonna explore the business side of innovation. And we'll start with the innovator's dilemma, which is what I described a moment ago. How big companies fail and why do they fail. And then we talk about the other side. So you have the existing companies, the entrenched companies that many times lose. But you have the new entrants that have to kind of get in and build a market. So we will look at both sides of the equation. Why these big companies can fail and why the new entrants have really hard time penetrating the market. So the two are mirror images of one another, and we're going to talk a lot about that.

And at the end, I'll spend, hopefully about a half an hour talking about a pretty radical idea on how a new startup or a new company can penetrate the market. And I will give you two examples that I personally was responsible for and show you how they work.

So that's The Innovator's Dilemma. Mr. Christensen did a revealing analysis of why these companies failed. And he took a very interesting industry to research, and that's the disk manufacturing. Hard disk manufacturing.

Now, he took it because his friend suggested that these are the fruit flies of business. Why fruit flies? Fruit flies are small flies. They live for a few days, which means you can create many, many generations in just a few months. So any genetic change that happens, you can see the implications of it over many, many generations by not having to wait 30 years for a generation, but just a few days and you can do that. So he was looking for same thing here. Can I look at an industry where it changes? What do you mean by changes? The leaders of yesterday are not the leaders of tomorrow, and it takes three years and suddenly the leaders disappear. There's a new set of companies that dominate the market. So he can look at why companies that were at the top of the hill, they were the big guys selling hard disk drives, suddenly lose to the next one. What happened?

So let's start. What do you think? Why do entrenched companies lose to the next one? Some say they get complacent. They think that they're untouchable. But I said at the beginning, these are smart people who built the company, and it's three years later and four years later, they're not getting complacent.

Sometimes it's difficult to predict where something is going. Like AI for example — we have an idea, but we don't know how far it's gonna go. So it could become obsolete very quickly. That's one of the things. And sometimes they have inventory or factories that they've spent so much money on that it just doesn't make financial sense to switch over. And sometimes the world is changing and so are the circumstances consisting of the company's success. So if you don't change or don't have available ways to change, you'll sometimes fail.

All of these reasons are correct. There are additional reasons we're gonna talk about. So let's take a breath. Will Tesla beat the rest of the car industry? We're in the middle of a revolution, right? In the middle of it. So while you are Ford and BMW and Volvo and whatever, and you have to ask yourself, "Am I gonna lose out to Tesla?" Yes or no? Your guess is my guess. We don't know yet. But I'm just showing you when you look at it — when it happens, it's suddenly like, I don't know.

Tesla owns today, I don't know, one percent of the car market, two percent of the car market. Chinese produce the same cars for a third of the price. We don't know. We just don't know. But you can start seeing how when it happens, it's so hard to predict.

Intel, they were at the top when they produced processors for PCs. All PCs had Intel processor, right? But what happened — now NVIDIA is on the top. Will they be the next processor of the world? We don't know. So I'm showing you things as they happen, and the question is: What's gonna happen? We don't know.

So let's look at the evolution of these drives. The first generation of these drives was developed by IBM and others for mainframe computers. Big computers fill out the whole room. IBM, the king of the hill. Second generation, minicomputers. Minicomputers were done in the Boston area, companies like Digital Equipment Corporation and others. That's the second generation. Third generation, personal computers.

And you can see that the big ones had a big disk — fourteen inch, then eight inch, then five and a quarter inch, three and a half inch for laptop computers. Then they went down to two and a half inches, then one point eight inch. And suddenly — portable hard monitoring. All the rest are computers. What is this?

When I was raising money back in the eighties, nineties, one of the investors that I worked with was working in this industry. They would buy the defunct companies. Remember that every generation, companies that were the leaders became defunct, and a new generation came of companies, not just products. So they were buying the old one. And he says, "You know why we were buying the old ones? Because people install these disks in other things, like in an X-ray machine or in a printing machine. And so they needed replacement parts. So we would buy the defunct company, fire everybody, and just hold the inventory and sell the inventory at five times the original price, because they had no choice." I said, "So why did you leave? It looks like a great business." He says, "Yeah. Did you ever walk into a room and tell everybody, 'Guys, we're very happy to buy all of you. You're all fired'?"

So let's look at the innovation. As you can see, the price per megabyte or gigabyte later fell through the floor throughout that period of time. Now, you don't even think about memory anymore, right? It's kind of cheap. But at that time, it started with $11,000 for a gigabyte down to pretty much nothing in '97. So it's a period of 10 years.

Yet, the disruptive parameter was not the ability to squeeze more memory onto this. So for that, we need to think about two terms: sustaining innovation versus disruptive innovation. And I suggest you also look at the link below. It's a very simple article to read. It summarizes the innovator's dilemma. By the way, the guy who wrote it, Christensen, was a professor at Harvard University, so you can find all of it.

What is sustaining innovation? When a company creates better performing products to sell for higher profits to its best customers. Give me examples. Tesla. Apple. Very good. iPhone, right? iPhone one, two, three, four, five, six, seven. And we're at 15 or something, right? What's the difference between them? Better camera, better this, better that. Nothing disruptive about this. But every year they come out with a new generation, right? Higher price, better performance. Flat TVs. What is the parameter? Size, right? Started with 30 inch. Now they are eighty-five inch, a hundred and fifty inch. And they now start including their streamer and whatever. All sustaining innovations.

I brought some very out-of-technology example. Herbal tea, Wissotzky. They want to capture as much of the shelf space in every store. So they have about 20 different herbal teas. They package them nicely, and they sell them for an exorbitant price, and they capture the market. One percent milk. Think about it. What do they do with all the fat they take out of the milk? Butter. Exactly. So they take out the good thing, make butter, make money, and sell it to you for a higher price. That's a sustaining innovation. Soy milk. All of these are sustaining innovations. They go to the same clients using the same infrastructure that you have already and bringing you more money. Typically, the strategy used by entrenched companies. And the main motive is, "I want to make more money using everything that I already do." That's sustaining innovation.

Now, what is disruptive innovation? Disruptive innovation is actually not what you think. I know all of you think disruptive means, wow, they came out with this great idea that nobody thought about and it's gonna change the world. It's not.

Disruptive innovation is when you get out of the normal standard measurements of how your products are measured. For example, in the disk drive — I put this little column in there. Size of the disk. What does size have to do with disk drives?

So when you have an eight inch drive, eight inch is about that size, big drive, and you have a PC, the eight inch drive just doesn't fit into it. But the PCs were just starting. We're talking about 1981. The industry just started, and then a company came and said, "I can do smaller ones." So the bigger ones didn't see that market coming. Same happens when they moved to laptops and so forth and so on. So what you see is disruptive means that suddenly the products or the solutions are measured or evaluated by a different parameter than the whole industry is working on. And we'll see more of it later on.

So it occurs when a new company with fewer resources moves into a market and later challenges an incumbent. And there are two disruptive events. The first one is easy to understand. Somebody says, "I can produce shirts for a lower price." Obviously, they disrupt the market. When would they be successful? They would be successful if they use their initial success in order to improve the product because they now have resources. They have a lot of customers who buy the shirts for $30, and they want to then start producing higher quality shirts for $35. So you start at the low end of the market, and you gradually take yourself up the market. That's a disruption of that level. You can see it in many, many industries.

The second is when a company creates a new segment in existing market by catering to some small opportunity. That's the reason why we included the 1.8 inch hard monitors. Later on, they use the same small disk in cameras, video cameras. So before they had solid state memory, they used very small disk. You can't put a five and a quarter inch or a three and a half inch or even a two and a half inch. So what happens is you come up with something that is different. It's different in ways that suddenly make them useful in areas that you didn't think about. But what they did later on is they kept improving those products. They start competing with the main industry on the parameters by which the main industry is measured. In this case, the cost per gigabyte.

So think about it. You enter somewhere, but you have to keep innovating using the standard measurements. So you pack more and more memory into this small disk. So the new innovations are usually inferior to existing ones measured by the industry standards. That's usually what happens, which is why the big companies look at it and say, "I don't know what to do with this."

So let's look at batteries. Because of the cell phones and laptops, the cost of energy density went down. So what we do is we have batteries that pack more and more power into the same space. So we talked that the phones and the laptops made the industry much more efficient. That's what brought the Tesla and the electric cars.

But what are the parameters that might disrupt this market? What else can disrupt that market? Something new. What else do you want from a battery? Charge time, right? How long it takes to charge the battery. With cars it's very, very critical. Because you drive, you wanna go into a gas station or a charging station, and you don't wanna wait there for an hour because you don't have an hour to wait. So charging time can be very disruptive.

But let's talk about it. What if you have a battery with very high energy density, but very long charge time — hours? In what ways can that change the industry? When you produce electricity, you have very, very big generators. You turn them on, you don't turn them off because it's very, very expensive to turn them on and turn them off. But demand fluctuates during the day. At 12 midnight, there's very little demand, and at 9:00 o'clock in the morning when everybody is turning on the air conditioning, there is a very high demand. That costs a tremendous amount of money because the electric companies have to have production capacity for the peak hours.

What happens if you have this kind of battery and people install it at home, turn it on at night when energy prices can be very, very low because there's no use, and in the morning instead of taking electricity from the grid, they take electricity from their home battery. So you create a whole different market where people will pay money for it. Because they can buy the electricity cheap at night and use it at home when electricity is expensive. Totally different. Why? Because you have something that is not useful for cars — it takes too long. It also opens up the ability to use it in places where the electricity production is not sustainable, like solar systems, like wind turbines. But if you can use it to charge and then release the energy when it's needed, then you have a whole different market. That's just an example.

Let's look at the second one. If you have relatively low energy density but very fast charging, the opposite — again, you can use it in many applications. What about structure? Let's assume that you could build a battery that you can mold and use as part of your... All of you here have laptops. What if the laptop itself, the enclosure, is a battery? What would that do?

What I'm trying to tell you is innovation many times is a different use of the technology that you have that compensates for the fact that it will not have the same energy density, that it will have other problems. But if it becomes popular and useful, then you have the resources to start improving the other parameters, and suddenly you have a product that completely disrupts the market. That's the way it works.

So let's look at examples of disruptive innovations. IBM personal computers. So they came up with this idea to do personal computers, but IBM was the king of the mainframe. They sold computers for millions of dollars, and somebody was playing with a toy called a personal computer. So they did two things. Number one is they said, "Oh, okay, forget about it. It's gonna be a toy." So the operating system, the DOS — "Well, I'll just take it from somebody." And then this young kid showed up. His name was Bill Gates. He says, "I have it. I can give it to you. Let's just sign this little deal that says that I own the operating system and I have the rights to distribute it wherever I want," and the rest is history.

Microsoft is worth, I don't know, ten times what IBM is worth. The other thing they did was they wanted to have an open architecture, which means they allowed everybody to build a PC compatible. So they opened up a whole industry, but they lost the industry. They had computers. They sold them to Lenovo. Everybody knows Lenovo used to be IBM. That's an example.

Xerox PARC, that's my favorite. Basically, the computers they use today were developed in the seventies by a group in Xerox Research Center called PARC, Palo Alto Research Center, and they developed pretty much everything you take today to be a computer as a minimum. The mouse, the windows, the menus, the WIMP — what you see is what you get. The fact that you look on the screen and you see the page the same way it's going to be printed. Laser printers, local area network, and there are a whole list. Basically, everything you use today was developed in Xerox PARC.

An amazing group of scientists and developers. And as Steve Jobs said, Xerox could have owned the entire computer industry. It would have been the IBM of the nineties and the Microsoft of the nineties. There are many, many articles trying to figure out how come Xerox missed the opportunity, because it was clear they developed amazing things.

And Bitcoin, blockchain — how disruptive is that going to be? They claim you don't need money anymore. What is Bitcoin used today for? Innovators need a niche market. It's not a very legal niche market, but it is a niche market and people use it, believe it or not. So here's a great example. I'm trying to show you innovations that are at the moment happening and we don't really know whether they're going to disrupt the market or not. It has very different parameters and strengths and weaknesses compared to paper money or government money, but we don't really know.

It is based on a technology called blockchain. Blockchain is not Bitcoin. It's a very different technology that is used by Bitcoin, and it's a very useful technology. Ten years ago, billions of dollars were invested in blockchain, and blockchain basically is a system by which you can produce documents and transactions that you can prove their authentication. They wanted to use that, for example, instead of the place where you register whether you bought a house or an apartment. Everything that you wanna have done in a way that cannot be forged and it cannot be erased. There is a big use for it, but the technology didn't go anywhere.

Here's a great example of that. I promised to talk again about Intel. So Intel was the king on the hill for PC processors. Pretty much every PC, including the Apple, had an Intel chip inside them. Then came the iPhone, and they didn't have the right processor for an iPhone, and they missed that market.

Then came NVIDIA. NVIDIA used to have graphic processors. If you look at your screen and you move the window, it just moves very nicely. You watch a video and it very smoothly plays on the computer. How does it do that? In all of your computers there is a special chip called the graphic processor done by NVIDIA, that does all the calculations needed in order to show all of these graphics.

These calculations are built on a vector processor. Vector processing is pretty basic technology, and NVIDIA built processors that are aimed at making those operations very, very fast. Then came the AI revolution that we talked about — ChatGPT and all of that — and it requires the same exact processing, and NVIDIA went through the roof. If you look at their stock price, they became a very big company over a few years. Again, the technology AI revolution became the enabler for NVIDIA. And Intel is stuck in the middle. Where is it gonna go? I'm just showing you how this company twice in its history missed when the market changed from beneath them, something it had no control over.

So what are the principles that Christensen came up with? It's very interesting. Principle number one is companies depend on existing customers to sustain and grow revenues. You ask why? They're not lazy. They're not full of themselves. But they focus on the thing that generates money, which is their customer. They listen and cater to their customer needs. What do customers want usually? Features, cost reduction, performance improvements. That's what most customers want, so that's what you do. If you're a good company, that's what you do. And you have an internal focus. Why? Because you're a big company. You have many people from manufacturing to marketing to whatever, and what you try to do is improve every operation so that you can make more money. That's what you do. Every single company in the world, because that's the right thing to do.

Second, small markets don't solve the growth needs of large companies. The IBM PC — it's a toy. I'm IBM, I sell one computer for millions of dollars. A PC that costs two thousand dollars is irrelevant to my bottom line. It's a rounding error. You know, I don't even see it in the financial reports, so I don't care about it. That's the reality. I'm a big company. I have ten billion dollars in revenues. Anything that is not in the hundreds of millions of dollars is just not interesting. That's why they miss it.

And this is exactly where a small startup can benefit. Why? Because they don't need and can't capture big established markets. A startup with a little bit of brain is not gonna go after the giants in their own turf. What do they do? They can thrive on relatively small market niches — what I call beachheads. They try to find a beachhead. They try to find somewhere that the big company ignored, couldn't fulfill, and you can do it. Because you only have fifty employees, you can be profitable and thrive. And they can innovate to cater to unmet needs. Why? Because they're a small company. They're very hungry — literally hungry. When you don't get salaries, you become really hungry. And they're willing to do anything, and they move fast. The big companies — it's not that they're idiots, they just — it's irrelevant in the big scheme. Most of these little niches remain little niches. That's what they are. They're small, and they remain small.

There is a reason why I showed you Bitcoin and all of that. We don't really know what's gonna be big or not. Which is — I told you — IBM licensing DOS for its personal computer. It's a toy. I don't care. I wanna move fast. I wanna get into the market. I wanna move on with life.

So if you are a small company, how do you find those beachheads? How do you find these customers that are not in the mainstream that might want and can use your technology or innovation? Markets that don't exist can't be analyzed. Can't say more than that. So if they don't exist, and you can't predict the market size, then you assume it is small. Big companies need big markets. So it's kind of just logic. How many people are gonna use the PC? I don't know. A thousand people, five thousand people. I can't really estimate. So you tend to estimate that it's zero, because you're a big company.

If you are the innovator, the little guy, you immediately assume you're going to sell billions of it. The big companies know it's hard to sell, so they assume it's gonna be a small market. That's just human nature. You ask why it happens — that's why it happens.

Organization capabilities define its disabilities. Sounds great, huh? What does that mean? Basically, it means that companies that succeeded are being good at what they do. They invest heavily in what makes them good. It's just logic. If I'm Kodak and I spent years developing all the chemicals and the ability to spread this chemical on a piece of celluloid — it's transparent, so I can do all of these phenomenal chemical things — that's what I work on. And I work on production, I work on improvements. That's what I do. Therefore, it's hard for them to change what they do. Their success DNA is embedded in everything they do.

And I can tell you something from my own company, ZoomInfo, which took me a while to understand what's going on. So what we were doing is a company that collected information about people and companies by crawling the internet, doing all kinds of language processing. And then we sold this data to sales and marketing organizations. Now, the business model that I chose — very early on I wanted the company to be profitable. For it to be profitable, we needed to generate cash. So if you charge $100 or you charge $10,000, which one would you charge? $10,000, right? So to charge $10,000, I need a salesman. So I hired salespeople. They started selling. The company was very successful. And we sold packages — I think the minimum was $1,800, right? But usually the salespeople pushed for $5,000 and up. Because otherwise you can't have salespeople.

And that bothered me. Because we missed the low end of the market. Not everybody can pay $5,000. So I wanted to develop a subset of the product for the low end of the market — $99 a month. Don't talk to anybody. Just put your credit card, boom, you're gone. So I introduced a product like that. It's not very complicated to think about how to do it. So instead of getting 1,000 records, you'll get 100 records. Very simple. And introduced it.

About a day after we introduced it, the salespeople came to my room and they said, "Listen, Yaron. You can do whatever you want. It's your company. But if you want me to meet my quota, which was a million dollar per salesman, I can't compete against myself." I said, "What happened?" He says, "Well, I had a deal for $10,000 with a customer. And he said, 'Oh, wow. I went on your website and I saw that there is a product that for $99 I can use it.' And I tried for half an hour to explain that this is a toy. This is the real product." The guy said, "Let me try the $99. And if it's not sufficient for me, I'll get back to you." He said, "I lost three deals today because of you. So you either take it out of the website or reduce my quota."

That was disappointing and embarrassing. So I did it. But I kept working on it. I came up with a different angle of the product. And introduced it. And what happened before happened again. I tried it six times. Six times. And I failed each and every time. Why? Because of that DNA. The company was built on direct sales. That's what I mean by the DNA of the company that goes across the board. Once you build a company and it's successful, you focus on increasing that success. If you introduce the disruptive technology, in most cases you compete against yourself and the organization will just stop you. I was the CEO of that company, and I couldn't get it done. So that's why big companies fail. They don't fail because they're idiots.

What happened? Competitors. If you look at the market today, there's Lusha, the Israeli guys. There's Apollo. And there are many, many competitors that came right in at the $99 a month. That's it. As trivial as can be. And they're very successful companies.

Kodak, they invented digital photography. They knew exactly what digital photography is. But their biggest investment was all their chemical know-how. They tried to use their chemical know-how and their chemical manufacturing capabilities in other areas. They just didn't find anything that was big enough to sustain an organization like Kodak. Blockbuster, we talked about it as well.

So you start seeing the inevitability of what happens, why these big companies lose the market. Principle number five — usually the innovators come in with something that is different, but it's different along a dimension that is not the main dimension. In disk drives, it was the disk size. If it's batteries, it might be all the things I said. And in ZoomInfo, it was the price. I couldn't compete against myself at a lower price, even if it is a smaller product. So you come in on a dimension that the bigger company just doesn't meet.

That forces the innovative company to search for a new breed of customers who would value the product not just by traditional properties. ZoomInfo — it was all the small salespeople, small organizations, one salesperson wanting to do something. They didn't want to commit to $5,000, $10,000. In the disk drive it was the size, whatever it is.

So let's be personal for a moment. Until now, you've heard about big companies, why they fail, what to do. Now you are the innovators. You want to start a company, and you want to be the one that builds a $10 billion company in three years. What do you need to do? If you're looking for an idea, what should you do?

So I'm showing you now four different things you can do. You want a disruptive innovation — we look at many, many business plans. There are two things that I always hear. I've yet to see a business plan that doesn't say, "We're going to disrupt the market." It's so overused, it's so not real. But everybody's looking to disrupt the market. Well, there are things that disrupt the market. I think that ChatGPT is one of those. It's too early to say where exactly it's going to disrupt the market and how, but it's very, very difficult to come up with a technology that you know is going to disrupt the market. And by the way, OpenAI, who developed this, raised $10 billion to begin with. So it wasn't like two kids sitting in the kitchen and disrupting the market. So my recommendation is — don't worry about this. Leave it alone.

Second is incremental innovation. So you're not gonna disrupt the market, but you will use existing technologies in a new way to improve a product or a process, or to solve a problem. So everything, all the pieces are here — you just put them in a way that brings different value. Gett. Nothing that Gett did was any smart innovation. They just replaced the taxi dispatcher that used to be all over the cities. There was a dispatcher that you would call a phone number and they would say, "Okay, I'll dispatch a cab for you." Nowadays you just don't have a dispatcher. Uber, Gett is the dispatcher. That's about it. But still a very nice company. Uber is the same. People had cars. People needed rides. Combine the two, done. Pango. Same thing. What do you have? You have GPS in the phone so you know how much to charge the person. There is a camera so the person who needs to check whether you are parked legally or not, takes a picture of your driving license. That connects immediately to the center and it says, "Yep, these guys are on Pango or not." Easy. Nothing in it is sophisticated. It's just using incremental innovation. I strongly recommend — if you find a new market, if you think you can do something about it, it's cheap to do.

Third one is enter an existing market by improving on existing offering. You don't even try to do something new. All you try is to do it better than the others. Facebook, as we said, it wasn't the first. You remember my philosophy about don't be the first? So Facebook was number 10. Google was number 10. Bookings.com — I don't remember what they were. All of these people came into an existing market with the same existing application. They just did it slightly better. They also were much smarter at marketing themselves.

And the last one, which I also strongly recommend, is enter an existing market with a new business model. Let's think about e-commerce. It's like going to a store. I sell the same shoes in the store or on Amazon. Same book, same detergent, same everything. What's the difference? Nothing. It's a business model. I can go on a computer, I select the product, I pay, somebody ships it to me. It's the business model that's different.

Netflix. I'll start with the early Netflix, not the Netflix of today. The early Netflix was exactly like Blockbuster. You wanted a video or a CD, you went on the web, you chose one, and they sent it to you — I think you could take four a month. Now, what's the benefit and what's the disadvantage? The disadvantage is they arrive when they arrive. So if you really felt like you need to see that movie now, it may not suit you. But if you said, "I don't care. I've ordered them, they will arrive, and I can watch them whenever I want, and I return them just by dropping them in a mailbox." It was slightly cheaper, but you had to commit to pay on a monthly basis whether you took movies or not.

But the benefit to Netflix was it reduced their inventory dramatically because you ship nationwide. And you can keep inventory of rare movies. If you have a store, you can't keep more than five thousand different titles because it's expensive. But if you have one center location where you can ship to anybody, you don't mind having ten thousand or a hundred thousand titles or movies, because even if somebody once a month wants it, they have it. That's how Netflix started. Different business model.

Question number three — do you know how to reach them? I gave you a list of 100 companies. Who are the companies? How am I gonna reach that person in a way that he or she will listen to me? I can send an email. Fine. You delete it before you even wake up, right? How do I do that?

Does anybody actively look for the product? A lot of innovations — the person you're trying to solve their problem for doesn't know they have a problem. Literally. Remember what I talked about the enablers in the beginning. There's so much technology today that makes it really simple to develop. But paying customers are hard to get. If I came to you and said, "Look, I have this great disruptive idea. It will cost you $1,000," you will say, "Uh, what?" Because people don't like to pay money for anything. You have to be convincing. And you don't control it. What I always tell engineers is that engineering is easy. You control all the parameters. Sales and marketing — you don't control anything. It's people that don't report to you. They either pay attention to you or don't pay attention to you. You don't control anything.

The first thing you want to do is think about your prospects and customers — who are they? How do you reach them? What do you tell them? How do you get them to buy from you? These are the questions, not the product. Product innovation is easy. Product selling is hard.

Now, why is it so important to sell the product? Most companies have employees. Most employees insist on getting their salaries on the first of the month. So if you wanna pay them, you need to get income. So you can go to investors and get money. The problem is that investors want also a return on their investment, and they are very finicky. In good times they will pour money at you. In bad times, like today, you can't get a penny. If your company gets to the point where you ran out of money, the company is closed. No employee will stay there.

That's the reality of life. You could have raised $10 million. You spent it in a year and a half with hiring 40 engineers developing something. You didn't sell anything, and your company is bankrupt and it's dead. You have to sell.

What is a brand? Something unique. A logo. Everybody knows what it is. It's something that you have specific feelings about that makes you do something. Like buy it. The identity of a company. The face of it. What you're interacting with as a customer. What you're being attracted to. You guys are in the right direction.

Does anybody here know who the Kardashians are? They've built themselves as a brand, so they've made their personality and their existence on this planet into something recognizable that they can monetize. If you ask what's specific about them, think about it. It is divorced from what they sell. They don't say, "BMW is cars." They are a brand. Everybody knows them. They have a positive attitude towards them, and people have no clue what they do. Remember that.

Who is the CEO of Toyota? Ford, BMW, Volvo, Mercedes? Tesla? Elon Musk. He's a brand. The guy is a genius at branding. A genius. But you can see the brand is divorced from the material. It's something on its own.

And what is a brand? You want the people you care about — because they are your customers — to know about you. You don't try to build a brand that everybody in the world knows. You want the people that will become your customers to know about you. And you said you wanna have a positive attitude. You want people to say, "I would like to work with this company," whatever they do.

In one of my companies, we talked about customer satisfaction. So I told them that I had a coordinator who said, "I hate this term, customer satisfaction." I said, "Excuse me. Why do you hate this term?" He said, "Because then you grade it from zero, when everybody hates you, to nine, they're okay with you, they're satisfied." He said, "I don't want any customer satisfaction." I said, "So what do you want?" He said, "Delight. I want people to be delighted about me."

What company has people stand from midnight waiting for the new whatever to come out? Apple. You see? It's emotional. You love them. You think they're geniuses. That's the hype of a brand. That's what you want. It's an emotion. It's not facts, it's emotion, and it has to relate to what you do somehow.

So now that I told you a little bit, how do you do it? It takes a long time. So when something takes a long time, you better start early. So remember what I said at the beginning — instead of building a company about the product, build it around the brand. So don't even start building your application. You're wasting your time. You're totally wasting your time.

What do you mean by build the company about the brand strategy? So one of the things I teach for my companies is this concept of branding first. You want to build an engine that will create this notion of a brand. So what do you do? How do you do that before having a product? So many times people ask, "Wait a minute, you want me to build a brand? What am I gonna sell? Because I don't have the product yet, because you told me not to develop the product but build the brand. But if I don't have a product, what am I talking about?"

You focus on the problem you try to solve instead of the solution. That's the main thing. So you're not talking about, "Here's how I solve your problem." You try to talk about the problem. And Google is your best friend. Regardless of what you do — you can develop a car, you can develop cosmetics, whatever it is — we all spend time on Google getting answers to some desired questions, right? So Google is your best friend, and everyone, including your prospect, is searching for answers to something on Google. So what you want is that somehow your customer, remember you need to build a brand that will talk to your customer, somehow they will get to you.

So one of the things we work on is what's called the long tail. Does anybody know what an SEO long tail is? SEO is search engine optimization. Basically, SEO means I want Google to present my page number one. That's SEO. Long word that's saying, "Get me first. Get me first. Get me first." That's what it means. I want to be first in Google.

Now, how do you do that? There are head keywords and there is long tail. What is a head keyword? It's common terms like necklace, laptop, car insurance, whatever it is. If you type in car insurance, you're gonna get every car insurance company in the world trying to compete to be first page. Everybody and his brother and his sister and his grandmother is gonna compete with you. So it's very, very hard because Google has long memory. Google will go with trusted sources. It has very high search volume, which is why people compete on it. Intense competition for first place and lower conversion rates because there's so much information — people just glimpse through it and don't click.

However, long tail is — you don't use one word, you use a phrase. Four to six words, like "eighteen inch silver necklace with a pendant." Who's gonna type that? Well, some people will. It has low search volume, less competition from Google because not a lot of people put this as a page title. And you have very high conversion rate because when people get to your page and they see "eighteen inch silver necklace with a pendant," they say, "Oh, that's exactly what I want." So you get a very high conversion rate. Seventy percent of the searches are long tail. Seventy percent.

What's the problem? The problem is that there are a million, million, million different combinations of words that people can type in, and you don't know it. As Chris Anderson of Wired magazine said, "The best way to dominate the web in the face of stiff competition is to optimize for long tail search."

Each keyword in the long tail has very few searches every month. If you want traffic, you need to have many, many combinations. So how do you effectively create hundreds if not millions of different pages? Blog. How many blogs can you write in an hour? How long do you think it will take to get to a thousand blogs on your website? Long time.

The database of information about something relevant to your problem. Why a database? Every line in the database can be a page, and every column is something you're gonna put on the page. Think about if you have a database about necklaces. You probably have in your store 5,000 different necklaces. You categorize them by pearls, and gold, and heavy gold. Database. For every single line in your database, you create a page. But then you can do better than that. You can take and turn it on its head.

For example, let's talk about an entity — person, address, company. It's a page on your website, and you can then turn the pages on their head. For example, I can talk about the 20 largest companies in New Haven, Connecticut, or in Ra'anana, or in Herzliya, or whatever. So you can create more content, and the more content you create automatically, the more chance you have for people who search for "companies in Herzliya" — Google will say, "That's the best answer I have. It's not the top 20, but it's companies in Herzliya. I'll give you this page." The more content you have that is unique, the more chances you're going to be first in some random searches.

Now, who is using long tail? Amazon — put anything you want, and if Amazon has it, you're gonna find it. LinkedIn — a page for every person, a page for every company. Crunchbase — a company about companies and their financing. Page for every company. Facebook — don't need to tell you about Facebook. TripAdvisor — a page per hotel, attraction, location. Zillow — they have a page for every single apartment and house in America, including my apartment in Boston with the wrong information. Very, very, very embarrassing.

So let's talk about, again, first movers. You see the problems. We talked about it. Nobody knows what they're doing. So let's talk a little bit about how we solve the problem. Let me show you the branding first solution.

It was founded in September 2019 by Ziv Segal and your humble presenter here, and it's tools for DevOps engineers to manage and optimize mission-critical Elasticsearch clusters. That was the business. So nobody understood what that meant. But that was what they wanted to solve.

Who are the prospects? We know — DevOps engineers. And how do we get to them? First of all, remember we said, "Can you prepare a list?" We don't know how to prepare a list of companies that use Elasticsearch. Real problem. So what do we do? We focus on the problem, not on the solution.

And so when Oxyl was founded, we had nothing to sell. The product vision was very murky. Founder Ziv came to me and says, "I've been working with Elasticsearch for seven years. It's a great, great product, but when it gets too much activity on the site, it breaks down." So we asked ourselves, "What would a DevOps engineer do when encountering a problem with their Elasticsearch installation?" I sat with Ziv for maybe two or three meetings. He kept asking me the same question — what do they do?

One day he came up and said, "Well, sometimes the system produces an error log, an error message, and it puts it in a log." I said, "Oh, interesting. Let's look at what they put out." So — could not lock, index writer is locked. Delaying allocation for underside shards. And the rest is mumbo jumbo like that. Total mumbo jumbo.

But let's look at what happened. So we created a long tail. For every single error log — and there are about 700 at the beginning — we created a page on our site. The title of the page was this obscure "could not lock, index writer is locked, whatever it is." And we put some explanation of what the error log is. And the result — Stack Overflow is the leading site where engineers get answers for questions. Elastic.com is the company that produces the Elasticsearch engine. And our response? Number one. Number one.

Why? Because nobody's gonna put a page on this stupid error message. So we wrote a script to extract all the error logs. Took Ziv about half an hour because it's open source. And today we have about 3,000 of them. We created a website with these 700 pages. We put additional detailed glossary and some basic terminology. It turns out there was no dictionary — no directory of what these terms are. And later on we added many how-tos.

Now what we found is that about 60 pages generated 80% of the traffic. Remember at the beginning we did everything automatically. So we generated 700 garbage pages — literally garbage pages. Why? Because it wasn't clear what the error log means even to us. We didn't understand what it was, but we published anyway. Once we got this, we said, "Okay, there are 60 pages we need to understand and write something intelligent about." That's what we did. Only 60, and we got the traffic.

Here is the traffic. Started in Q4 2020 — that was right at the beginning. And in Q4 2022, we had about 100,000 visitors per month, 300,000 per quarter. That's how it builds.

But traffic is not yet leads. Remember, we need to sell. So you need to have a marketing funnel. So what we did is we developed a little bit of a free tool that would allow customers to check something about their system — a free checkup. The user needed to create an account to run the checkup. And we got many people per quarter to use this. So we moved from "who the hell are these DevOps for Elasticsearch" to having a list of people who already used our product, and we started to develop with them. And that's before we had a product. You start understanding what I'm talking about? You start thinking about a brand before you start developing a product.

What happened next? In November '23, the company was acquired by Elastic. Four years. Very good money. They took the company and the founders, Ziv and myself, to be acquired. And one of the main reasons for the acquisition was the content that we created. Later on when we were acquired, we were able to see what they were writing about Elasticsearch. And the main thing was that they were furious that most of their customers were quoting our content, and that their own support engineers were sending customers to our site to get answers. That really, really hurt. So they decided it is much better to own us than to fight against us.

Here's an example of the power of branding and marketing first and long-term SEO. And that's kind of the end today.

Summary. What we wanted to talk about is move from all kinds of what happens to IBM and Google and whatever to — you wanna start a company, what to do. The business of introducing new products. We talked about the innovator's dilemma. We talked about the big company, the sustaining innovation versus disruptive innovation. Really think about it. Spend some time looking at your presentation later on. And you have here the five principles we discussed.

And your biggest challenge is not to build the product, but to bring paying customers. That's the main thing I want you to take away from this. Everything I can say about innovation — at the end it will bring you no money. Think about how you sell. That's the greatest innovation you can do. Thank you.

Netflix המוקדמת הייתה כמו Blockbuster, אבל במודל אחר: בוחרים באתר, מקבלים בדואר, מחזירים בדואר ומשלמים מנוי חודשי. היתרון ל-Netflix היה מלאי נמוך בהרבה ומבחר גדול בהרבה ממיקום מרכזי אחד.

Android הוא דוגמה למודל עסקי שונה. Apple מוכרת פתרון סגור: iPhone ו-iOS רק על מכשירי Apple. Google רכשה את Android ונתנה ליצרנים להשתמש במערכת ההפעלה בחינם. איפה היא מרוויחה? Google Play ושירותים אחרים. זה דומה למלחמה הישנה בין Microsoft ו-Apple: Microsoft נתנה ל-Windows לרוץ על כל מחשב, Apple שמרה מערכת סגורה. כאן Google עשתה את אותו דבר בסמארטפונים, אפילו בחינם.

אם יש לכם רעיון, תשאלו: האם אתם יכולים להסביר אותו בפחות מחמש מילים באנגלית? ככל שהחדשנות מתוחכמת ומשבשת יותר, קשה יותר לאנשים להבין למה אכפת להם. כולנו עסוקים ומוצפים בפרסום ומסרים. אם אני לא מבין בחמש מילים, איבדתם אותי.

כשיש רעיון חדש, שאלו את עצמכם: האם יש לכם היכרות אינטימית עם הבעיה והשוק? למשל Gett: האם אתם מבינים איך נהגי מוניות מרוויחים, מה ההוצאות שלהם, מה מכעיס אותם? מתברר ש-Gett מכעיסה אותם כי היא גובה 1,000 שקלים בחודש גם אם הנהג חולה, במילואים או בבית. חייבים להבין את הדינמיקה.

האם אתם יכולים לרשום שמות של לפחות 100 לקוחות פוטנציאליים, חברות ואנשים? בעיקר ב-B2B. הרבה יזמים נשארים עם מבט ריק כששואלים אותם. הם אומרים: "כל מי ש..." ואני אומר: תן שם. אם אינכם יודעים שמות, איך תגיעו אליהם? אם אין רשימה, אינכם מבינים את השוק ברמה בסיסית.

האם אתם יודעים איך להגיע אליהם? גם אם יש רשימת חברות, איך תגרמו לאדם להקשיב? אפשר לשלוח מייל, אבל הוא יימחק לפני שהתעוררתם. האם מישהו מחפש באופן פעיל את המוצר? בהרבה חדשנויות האדם שאתם פותרים לו בעיה לא יודע שיש לו בעיה. בדיעבד זה נראה ברור, אבל בזמן ההמצאה לא. דוגמה: tissues הומצאו להסרת איפור, והחברות הופתעו שאנשים משתמשים בהם גם לקינוח אף.

האתגר הגדול ביותר אינו לבנות את המוצר. בניית Pango, Uber או Gett היא קלה יחסית עם ה-enablers של היום. יש AWS, שפות תכנות, מערכות הפעלה, הכול קל וזול. הבעיה היא להשיג לקוחות משלמים. אנשים לא אוהבים לשלם כסף. צריך לשכנע אותם. בהנדסה אתם שולטים בפרמטרים; בשיווק ומכירות אינכם שולטים בכלום. אנשים שלא עובדים אצלכם מחליטים אם להקשיב או לקנות.

לכן הדבר הראשון הוא לחשוב על prospects ו-customers: מי הם, איך מגיעים אליהם, מה אומרים להם, ואיך גורמים להם לקנות. אלה השאלות, לא המוצר. Product innovation קל. Product selling קשה.

למה כל כך חשוב למכור? כי לעובדים יש נטייה לדרוש משכורת בראשון לחודש. כדי לשלם צריך הכנסות. אפשר ללכת למשקיעים, אבל משקיעים רוצים תשואה והם הפכפכים. בזמנים טובים הם זורקים כסף, בזמנים רעים כמו היום קשה להשיג שקל. אם נגמר הכסף, החברה נסגרת. גם אם גייסתם עשרה מיליון דולר, בזבזתם בשנה וחצי על ארבעים מהנדסים ולא מכרתם, החברה מתה. חייבים למכור.

לכן במקום לבנות חברה סביב רעיון מוצר, בנו אותה סביב branding ו-marketing strategy. מהו brand? זה משהו ייחודי, לוגו, זהות של חברה, הפנים שלה, מה שהלקוח מתקשר איתו ומה שמושך אותו. אבל חשוב יותר: brand הוא רגש ויחס. Kardashians בנו את עצמם כ-brand; האישיות והקיום שלהם הפכו למשהו שאפשר למנף. מי מנכ"ל Toyota, Ford, BMW או Volvo? רובכם לא יודעים. מי מנכ"ל Tesla? Elon Musk. הוא brand. גאון במיתוג. brand מנותק במידה מסוימת מהחומר עצמו.

אתם רוצים שהאנשים שחשובים לכם, הלקוחות שלכם, יכירו אתכם ויחשבו עליכם חיובית. לא צריך שכל העולם יכיר. צריך שהלקוחות העתידיים יגידו: הייתי רוצה לעבוד עם החברה הזו. בחברה אחת דיברנו על customer satisfaction, ומישהו אמר שהוא שונא את המונח כי הוא מודד מסולם שבו אפס שונאים אותך ותשע מרוצים ממך. הוא אמר: אני לא רוצה satisfaction, אני רוצה delight. Apple גורמת לאנשים לעמוד מחצות למוצר חדש. זה רגש. brand הוא רגש, לא רק עובדות, והוא צריך להיות קשור למה שאתם עושים.

איך עושים את זה? זה לוקח זמן, ולכן צריך להתחיל מוקדם. במקום לבנות חברה סביב המוצר, בנו סביב brand. אל תתחילו אפילו לפתח את האפליקציה; אתם מבזבזים זמן. מה פירוש brand strategy לפני מוצר? אני מלמד חברות שלי branding first: לבנות מנוע שיוצר תפיסת brand. אבל אם אין מוצר, על מה מדברים? מתמקדים בבעיה שאתם מנסים לפתור במקום בפתרון.

Google הוא החבר הכי טוב שלכם. לא משנה אם אתם מפתחים רכב, קוסמטיקה או תוכנה, אנשים מחפשים תשובות בגוגל. גם הלקוחות הפוטנציאליים שלכם מחפשים משהו. אתם רוצים שהם יגיעו אליכם.

כאן נכנס SEO long tail. SEO פירושו search engine optimization: לגרום לגוגל להציג את הדף שלי ראשון. יש head keywords ויש long tail. Head keywords הם מילים נפוצות כמו necklace, laptop, car insurance. אם תכתבו car insurance, כל חברות הביטוח בעולם יתחרו על המקום הראשון. התחרות עזה, Google מעדיף מקורות אמינים ותיקים, וההמרה נמוכה כי אנשים רק מדפדפים.

Long tail הוא ביטוי של ארבע עד שש מילים, למשל "eighteen inch silver necklace with a pendant". מעט אנשים יחפשו בדיוק כך, אבל התחרות נמוכה וה-conversion גבוה, כי מי שמגיע לדף כזה רואה בדיוק את מה שחיפש. שבעים אחוז מהחיפושים הם long tail. הבעיה היא שיש מיליוני קומבינציות, ואתם לא יודעים אותן. Chris Anderson מ-Wired אמר שהדרך הטובה לשלוט באינטרנט מול תחרות קשה היא לאופטימיזציה לחיפושי long tail.

כל keyword כזה מביא מעט חיפושים, ולכן צריך הרבה מאוד קומבינציות. איך יוצרים מאות או מיליוני דפים? בלוג? כמה פוסטים אפשר לכתוב בשעה? ייקח שנים להגיע לאלף. הפתרון הוא database של מידע רלוונטי לבעיה. כל שורה במסד הנתונים יכולה להיות עמוד, וכל עמוד יכול למשוך חיפוש long tail. אם יש חנות עם 5,000 שרשראות, כל שרשרת היא עמוד עם קטגוריות כמו pearls, gold, heavy gold. אפשר גם להפוך את המידע וליצור עמודים כמו "20 החברות הגדולות בניו הייבן" או "חברות בהרצליה". ככל שיש יותר תוכן ייחודי, גדל הסיכוי ש-Google יציג אתכם בחיפושים ספציפיים.

מי משתמש ב-long tail? Amazon: כל מוצר הוא עמוד. LinkedIn: עמוד לכל אדם ולכל חברה. Crunchbase: עמוד לכל חברה ומימון. Facebook, TripAdvisor, Zillow — לכל נכס וכתובת יש עמוד, גם אם המידע שגוי. זה הכוח של long tail.

אז איך פותרים את בעיית ה-first mover והחדירה לשוק? הנה פתרון branding first. Opster נוסדה בספטמבר 2019 על ידי Ziv Segal ועל ידי, והציעה כלים ל-DevOps engineers לנהל ולבצע אופטימיזציה ל-Elasticsearch clusters קריטיים. אף אחד לא הבין מה זה אומר, אבל זו הייתה הבעיה שרצינו לפתור.

מי הלקוחות הפוטנציאליים? DevOps engineers. איך מגיעים אליהם? לא ידענו להכין רשימה של חברות שמשתמשות ב-Elasticsearch. אז התמקדנו בבעיה ולא בפתרון. כשהחברה נוסדה לא היה לנו מה למכור, וחזון המוצר היה מעורפל. Ziv אמר לי: עבדתי עם Elasticsearch שבע שנים. זה מוצר נהדר, אבל כשהאתר מקבל יותר מדי פעילות הוא נשבר. שאלנו: מה עושה DevOps engineer כשהוא נתקל בבעיה בהתקנת Elasticsearch?

בכמה פגישות Ziv חזר על השאלה. יום אחד הוא אמר: לפעמים המערכת מייצרת error log או הודעת שגיאה ושמה אותה בלוג. אמרתי: מעניין, בוא נסתכל. הודעות כמו "could not lock, index writer is locked" או "delaying allocation for unassigned shards" ושאר ג'יבריש. אבל כאן קרה משהו חשוב.

יצרנו long tail. עבור כל error log, ובתחילה היו בערך 700, יצרנו עמוד באתר. כותרת העמוד הייתה הודעת השגיאה האפלה עצמה, ושמנו הסבר כלשהו. Stack Overflow הוא האתר המוביל למהנדסים לקבל תשובות, Elastic.com היא החברה שמייצרת Elasticsearch, אבל התוצאה שלנו הייתה מספר אחת. למה? כי אף אחד לא שם עמוד על הודעת שגיאה כל כך ספציפית. Ziv כתב סקריפט שחילץ את כל error logs מהקוד הפתוח, וזה לקח לו חצי שעה. היום יש אלפים כאלה. יצרנו אתר עם 700 עמודים, glossary מפורט ומונחים בסיסיים, ובהמשך הוספנו how-tos.

גילינו שכ-60 עמודים יצרו 80% מהטראפיק. בהתחלה עשינו הכול אוטומטית ויצרנו 700 עמודי זבל, ממש זבל, כי אפילו אנחנו לא הבנו את הודעות השגיאה. אבל פרסמנו בכל זאת. אחרי שראינו אילו 60 עמודים מביאים תנועה, אמרנו: את אלה צריך להבין ולכתוב עליהם משהו חכם. רק 60 עמודים הביאו את רוב הטראפיק.

הטראפיק התחיל ברבעון הרביעי של 2020, וברבעון הרביעי של 2022 היו בערך 100,000 מבקרים בחודש, 300,000 ברבעון. כך זה נבנה. אבל טראפיק אינו leads. צריך למכור. לכן פיתחנו כלי חינמי קטן, free checkup, שאפשר ללקוחות לבדוק משהו במערכת שלהם. כדי להריץ אותו המשתמש היה צריך לפתוח חשבון. כך עברנו מ"מי לעזאזל הם ה-DevOps האלה ל-Elasticsearch" לרשימה של אנשים שכבר השתמשו במוצר שלנו. וזה קרה לפני שהיה לנו מוצר. מתחילים להבין? חושבים על brand לפני שמפתחים מוצר.

מה קרה אחר כך? בנובמבר 2023 החברה נרכשה על ידי Elastic. ארבע שנים, סכום יפה. הם קנו את החברה ואת המייסדים, Ziv ואותי. אחת הסיבות המרכזיות לרכישה הייתה התוכן שיצרנו. אחרי הרכישה ראינו מה Elastic כתבו על Elasticsearch, והדבר העיקרי היה שהם כעסו מאוד שרוב הלקוחות שלהם ציטטו את התוכן שלנו, ואפילו מהנדסי התמיכה שלהם שלחו לקוחות לאתר שלנו לקבל תשובות. זה כאב להם מאוד. לכן הם החליטו שעדיף לקנות אותנו מאשר להילחם בנו.

זו דוגמה לכוח של branding ו-marketing first, ול-SEO ארוך טווח. וזה בערך סוף השיעור היום.

לסיכום, רצינו לעבור מהשאלה מה קורה ל-IBM, Google וחברות גדולות אחרות, לשאלה: אם אתם רוצים להקים חברה, מה עושים? דיברנו על העסק של הכנסת מוצרים חדשים לשוק. דיברנו על Innovator's Dilemma, על חברות גדולות, על sustaining innovation מול disruptive innovation. תחשבו על זה, תעברו על המצגת, ויש כאן את חמשת העקרונות שדיברנו עליהם.

האתגר הגדול ביותר שלכם הוא לא לבנות את המוצר, אלא להביא לקוחות משלמים. זה הדבר המרכזי שאני רוצה שתיקחו מהשיעור. כל מה שאומר על חדשנות לא יביא לכם כסף אם לא תחשבו איך למכור. זו החדשנות הגדולה ביותר שאתם יכולים לעשות. תודה.
english_summary:
This lecture focuses on product innovation and the business challenge of moving an idea into the market. It begins by reviewing the previous lecture's argument that innovation is usually incremental and enabled by prior technologies, then shifts to Clayton Christensen's Innovator's Dilemma. The key question is why successful, well-managed incumbent companies often fail when disruptive innovations appear. The hard disk drive industry is used as a fast-moving case study: each generation of smaller drives created new markets and displaced companies that had dominated the previous generation.

The lecture distinguishes sustaining innovation from disruptive innovation. Sustaining innovation improves products for existing customers using familiar metrics such as performance, quality, features, or price. Disruptive innovation is different: it enters through a new parameter that incumbents do not value at first, such as disk size, battery charge time, form factor, or lower price. These products may look inferior according to the old industry's standards, but they open new use cases and can later improve enough to challenge the mainstream market. Examples include IBM PCs, Xerox PARC, Bitcoin and blockchain, NVIDIA's rise through AI workloads, and ZoomInfo's inability to serve the low end of the market because its direct-sales DNA blocked a cheaper self-service product.

The practical message for startups is that building the product is usually easier than finding paying customers. Entrepreneurs can pursue incremental innovation, improve an existing offering, or enter a market with a new business model rather than chasing the fantasy of obvious disruption. They must understand the customer, name real prospects, know how to reach them, and explain the product in a few words. The lecture then argues for a branding-first strategy: focus on the customer problem before the solution, use Google and SEO long-tail content to attract prospects, and create demand before the product is complete. The Opster/Elasticsearch case shows how hundreds of error-log pages, a glossary, how-to content, and a free checkup tool built traffic, leads, brand authority, and eventually contributed to acquisition by Elastic.

ההרצאה עוסקת בחדשנות מוצרית ובאתגר העסקי של העברת רעיון לשוק. היא נפתחת בסיכום ההרצאה הקודמת: חדשנות היא בדרך כלל תהליך הדרגתי שמופעל על ידי טכנולוגיות ותנאים מאפשרים. משם היא עוברת ל־The Innovator's Dilemma של Clayton Christensen ולשאלה מדוע חברות גדולות ומנוהלות היטב נכשלות כאשר מופיעה חדשנות משבשת. תעשיית הדיסקים הקשיחים משמשת כמקרה מבחן מהיר: כל דור של דיסקים קטנים יותר יצר שוק חדש והדיח חברות שהובילו את הדור הקודם.

ההרצאה מבחינה בין sustaining innovation לבין disruptive innovation. חדשנות משמרת משפרת מוצרים עבור לקוחות קיימים לפי מדדים מוכרים כמו ביצועים, איכות, פיצ'רים או מחיר. חדשנות משבשת נכנסת דרך ממד אחר שהחברות הגדולות אינן מעריכות בתחילה: גודל פיזי, זמן טעינה, צורה או מחיר נמוך. בהתחלה המוצר נראה נחות לפי המדדים הישנים, אבל הוא פותח שימושים חדשים ובהמשך משתפר עד שהוא מאיים על השוק המרכזי. הדוגמאות כוללות את IBM PC, Xerox PARC, Bitcoin ו־blockchain, עליית NVIDIA בזכות AI, ו־ZoomInfo שלא הצליחה לשרת את השוק הזול בגלל ה־DNA הארגוני של מכירות ישירות.

המסר המעשי לסטארטאפים הוא שבניית המוצר בדרך כלל קלה יותר מהבאת לקוחות משלמים. יזמים יכולים לבחור חדשנות אינקרמנטלית, שיפור הצעה קיימת או כניסה לשוק עם מודל עסקי חדש, במקום לרדוף אחרי פנטזיה של disruption ברור. צריך להבין את הלקוח, לדעת לנקוב בשמות לקוחות אמיתיים, לדעת איך להגיע אליהם ולהסביר את המוצר בכמה מילים. ההרצאה מציעה אסטרטגיית branding first: להתמקד בבעיה של הלקוח לפני הפתרון, להשתמש ב־Google וב־SEO long tail כדי למשוך prospects, ולבנות ביקוש לפני שהמוצר שלם. הדוגמה של Opster ו־Elasticsearch מראה כיצד עמודי error logs, glossary, how-to content וכלי free checkup יצרו טראפיק, לידים, סמכות מותגית ובסוף תרמו לרכישה על ידי Elastic.
